opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think logic-based AI has gotten a somewhat unfair reputation in recent years, partly because the old-school expert systems of the seventies and eighties were so brittle. You'd hand-code a bunch of rules, and the system would fall apart the moment it hit something its programmers hadn't anticipated. People looked at that and concluded logic was a dead end, and then deep learning came along and swept the field.

But I think that's the wrong lesson. The problem with those early systems wasn't logic per se. It was that the knowledge was hand-coded, the reasoning was crisp rather than uncertain, and there was no real learning or grounding in experience. If you take logic and make it probabilistic, so you're reasoning about degrees of truth and confidence rather than just true or false, and you let the system learn its knowledge from data and interaction rather than having humans type it in, it becomes a very different and much more powerful beast. That's what we've tried to do with Probabilistic Logic Networks in the OpenCog framework, and now in OpenCog Hyperon.

On the other hand, I don't think logic alone is going to get you to AGI either, any more than neural nets alone will. The human mind isn't a theorem prover. A lot of what we do is pattern recognition, association, perception, evolutionary-style creative recombination of ideas. So my view has always been that you need an integrative architecture, where logical reasoning is one cognitive process among several, all acting on a shared knowledge representation and helping each other out. I call that cognitive synergy. When the pattern recognizer gets stuck, the reasoner can help it. When the reasoner faces a combinatorial explosion, which is the classic problem with logic, then learned heuristics and attention allocation can guide it toward the inferences that matter.

And in the current moment with large language models, I think logic matters more, not less. LLMs are remarkable, but they're weak at reliable multi-step reasoning, at knowing what they don't know, and at generalizing far beyond their training distribution. Those are exactly the things a well-designed uncertain reasoning system is good at. So I see logic-based methods as a crucial ingredient, not the whole recipe, in getting from where we are now to genuinely general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response presents logic as one process in an integrated architecture, but does not describe it as an abstract reasoning module largely independent of its neural substrate.

r002.rationale: It mentions perception and learning from interaction, but does not state that human logical reasoning ultimately draws its knowledge from perception and action.

r003.rationale: It criticizes hand-coded knowledge in early systems, but does not say that commonsense knowledge is too extensive to encode by hand.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes logic as a reasoning process from hand-coded knowledge, arguing that a system can learn its knowledge from data and interaction.

r005.rationale: It discusses LLMs’ reasoning weaknesses, but not translating natural language into formal logic to populate a knowledge base.

r006.rationale: It mentions combinatorial explosion as a challenge for logic, but not the unresolved inference-scaling problem after acquiring a vast corpus of logical expressions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think logic-based AI has gotten a bad rap that it only partly deserves. If you look back at the history of the field, what people call "good old-fashioned AI" or GOFAI was, in a lot of ways, a very narrow version of what logic can actually do. It was mostly crisp first-order logic, hand-coded rules, no real way to handle uncertainty, no real learning. And when that failed to scale, people threw the whole paradigm out, which I think was an overreaction.

My own view, and this is what I've been pursuing with OpenCog for a long time now, is that logic is one of several necessary components, but it's not sufficient on its own. The human mind clearly does something like reasoning. We form abstractions, we chain inferences together, we generalize from a few examples in ways that look very much like inductive and abductive inference. A purely neural approach, at least as we currently understand it, is pretty weak at those things. Large language models can mimic reasoning, but they do it in a way that's shallow and brittle once you get outside the distribution of what they've seen.

So the question for me isn't logic versus no logic, it's what kind of logic, and how is it integrated with everything else. In our work we use probabilistic logic, specifically what we call Probabilistic Logic Networks, where every statement carries truth values with uncertainty and confidence attached. That lets you reason under the kind of messy, incomplete knowledge that real agents actually have. And critically, the logic engine doesn't operate in a vacuum. It sits in a shared knowledge store alongside evolutionary learning, neural pattern recognition, attention allocation, and so on. Each of those processes can feed into and modify the others. That's what I mean when I talk about cognitive synergy.

Where I think pure logic-based approaches go wrong is when they assume you can hand-build enough axioms to cover the world, or that symbol grounding will just take care of itself. You need perception, you need embodiment or at least rich interaction with an environment, and you need the system to learn its own concepts rather than inherit them from a programmer. Logic is great for manipulating representations, but something else has to create those representations in the first place.

The other thing I'd say is that the current excitement around deep learning has actually made the case for logic stronger, not weaker, in a funny way. When you see how much compute these systems burn to do things a child does trivially, and how they still fail at basic consistency and multi-step reasoning, it becomes pretty clear that a more structured, symbolic layer is going to be part of the answer. Whether that gets implemented as explicit logical inference, or as something that emerges inside neural architectures, or as a hybrid like what we're building, I think is still an open question. But I'd bet on the hybrid.

r001.rationale: The response describes older logic-based AI as narrow and advocates integrating logic with neural and other processes, but does not say it sought to implement advanced reasoning as a module independent of its neural substrate.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems need perception, embodiment, and interaction, but does not state that human logical reasoning draws its knowledge from perception and action.

r003.rationale: It criticizes the assumption that enough axioms can be hand-built, but does not identify the volume of commonsense knowledge as exceeding what is feasible to encode by hand.

r004.rationale: The response favors logic as one component in a hybrid system and criticizes hand-building axioms, but does not clearly distinguish using logical inference as an AGI’s core mechanism from requiring hand-coded knowledge.

r005.rationale: The response does not describe translating natural language into formal logic to populate a knowledge base.

r006.rationale: The response does not discuss acquiring a large corpus of logical expressions or the difficulty of scaling inference over it.

astra-6.text:
I think logic-based AI has an important role to play, but I’m skeptical that it’s sufficient on its own. Logic is a powerful way of representing abstractions and making chains of reasoning explicit. But an intelligent system also has to figure out which abstractions are useful, which premises to consider, and which inference to make next. The rules of logic don’t, by themselves, give you an efficient way to do that.

If you look at human thought, some of it resembles logical reasoning, but a lot of it is associative, perceptual, intuitive. You recognize a pattern, you get a hunch, and then perhaps you use reasoning to elaborate it or check it. I think an AGI needs that sort of interaction between different cognitive processes.

There’s also a distinction between classical logic, where propositions are true or false, and forms of reasoning that deal with uncertainty. In the real world, almost everything you know is provisional and context-dependent. So I’m more interested in logic that can operate with uncertain knowledge and work together with learning.

The challenge is making those pieces help each other. Learning should guide reasoning toward promising directions, and reasoning should help learning generalize beyond the examples it has seen. So I wouldn’t dismiss logic-based AI at all. I’d put it inside a broader cognitive architecture rather than expect logic alone to carry the whole burden of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses logic as part of a broader cognitive architecture, but does not describe it as an abstract reasoning module independent of a neural substrate.

r002.rationale: It says human thought includes perceptual and associative processes, but does not state that logical reasoning gets its knowledge from perception and action.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the scale of commonsense knowledge or the feasibility of hand-coding it.

r004.rationale: It argues that logic alone is insufficient, but does not distinguish logic as the core mechanism from the need for hand-coded knowledge.

r005.rationale: It does not mention using LLMs to translate natural language into formal logic or populate a knowledge base.

r006.rationale: It does not address the difficulty of scaling inference over a large corpus of logical expressions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think logic has an important role to play, but I’m skeptical that you get to AGI by making logic the whole architecture. There’s a big difference between having a system that can derive conclusions from a carefully specified set of premises and having a system that can figure out which concepts and premises are useful in a messy world.

If you already have the right representation, logical inference can be very powerful. But where does that representation come from? How does the system connect its symbols to perception and action? How does it decide which of a million possible inferences is worth making? Those are central parts of intelligence, and a logical calculus by itself doesn’t resolve them.

I’m more interested in an architecture where reasoning interacts with learning, perception, memory, and motivation. You want uncertain, revisable reasoning, because almost everything an intelligent system knows about the world is provisional. And you want other processes that can discover patterns and create abstractions that the reasoning system can then work with.

So I wouldn’t dismiss logic-based AI. I’d say logic is a valuable component, but the interesting question is how it participates in a larger cognitive system.
